From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Swedish artist (1862–1944)

"af Klint" redirects here. For other uses, see [af Klint (disambiguation)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Af_Klint_(disambiguation) "Af Klint (disambiguation)").

**Hilma af Klint** (Swedish:[[ˈhɪ̂lːma ˈɑːv ˈklɪnːt]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Swedish "Help:IPA/Swedish"); 26 October 1862 – 21 October 1944) was a Swedish [artist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artist "Artist") and [mystic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mysticism "Mysticism") whose paintings are considered to be among the first major [abstract](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstract_art "Abstract art") works in Western art history.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-1) A considerable body of her work predates the first purely abstract compositions by [Kandinsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wassily_Kandinsky "Wassily Kandinsky"), [Malevich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazimir_Malevich "Kazimir Malevich"), and [Mondrian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piet_Mondrian "Piet Mondrian").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-TATE-2) She belonged to a group called "The Five", a circle of women inspired by [Theosophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theosophy "Theosophy") who shared a belief in the importance of trying to contact the "[High Masters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masters_of_the_Ancient_Wisdom "Masters of the Ancient Wisdom")", often through [séances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A9ance "Séance").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-3) Her paintings, which sometimes resemble diagrams, were a visual representation of complex spiritual ideas.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-4)

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hilma_af_Klint&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/94/Eftersommar_Hilma_af_Klint_1903.jpeg/500px-Eftersommar_Hilma_af_Klint_1903.jpeg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Eftersommar_Hilma_af_Klint_1903.jpeg)

_Eftersommar_ (_Late Summer_) an early naturalistic work, painted by af Klint in 1903, an example of the works she exhibited to the public during her lifetime

Hilma af Klint was the fourth child of Mathilda ([née](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_name#Maiden_and_married_names "Birth name")Sonntag) and Captain Victor af Klint, a Swedish naval commander. The family surname is 'af Klint', _af_ being a Swedish [nobiliary particle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobiliary_particle "Nobiliary particle"). She spent summers with her family at their manor, "Hanmora", on the island of [Adelsö](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adels%C3%B6 "Adelsö") on [Lake Mälaren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_M%C3%A4laren "Lake Mälaren"). In these idyllic surroundings, she came into contact with nature at an early age. Her experience of natural forms became an inspiration in her work, and she later lived on [Munsö](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muns%C3%B6 "Munsö"), an island next to Adelsö.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Af Klint showed a great interest in [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics "Mathematics") and [botany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Botany "Botany") and an ability in visual art. After the family moved to Stockholm, she studied at _Tekniska skolan_ (Technical School, now [Konstfack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Konstfack "Konstfack")) in Stockholm, where she studied portraiture and landscape painting.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-:1-5)

Af Klint was admitted to the [Royal Academy of Fine Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Swedish_Academy_of_Fine_Arts "Royal Swedish Academy of Fine Arts") at the age of twenty.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-:0-6) Between 1882 and 1887, she studied portrait painting, botanical drawing, and landscape painting.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-:1-5) She graduated with honors and was granted a scholarship in the form of a studio in the "Atelier Building" (Ateljébyggnaden) owned by the Academy of Fine Arts between [Hamngatan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamngatan "Hamngatan") and [Kungsträdgården](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kungstr%C3%A4dg%C3%A5rden "Kungsträdgården") in central Stockholm, which was the main cultural hub in the Swedish capital at that time. The same building also held [Blanch's Café](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blanch's_Caf%C3%A9 "Blanch's Café") and Blanch's Art Gallery, where conflict arose between the conventional views of the Academy of Fine Arts and the opposition movement of the Art Society ([Konstnärsförbundet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Konstn%C3%A4rsf%C3%B6rbundet "Konstnärsförbundet")), inspired by the French [_plein air_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/En_plein_air "En plein air") painters. Af Klint began working in Stockholm, gaining recognition for her landscapes, botanical drawings, and portraits.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-7) Her conventional painting was a source of income, but her abstract remained a separate practice.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-8)

## Spiritual and philosophical ideas

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hilma_af_Klint&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Spiritual and philosophical ideas")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6d/Hilma-af-Klint.jpg/250px-Hilma-af-Klint.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hilma-af-Klint.jpg)

af Klint in her studio, c. 1895

In 1880, af Klint's younger sister Hermina died. Around this time, the spiritual dimension of her life had begun to develop.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-9) Af Klint's interest in abstraction and symbolism grew from her involvement in [spiritism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kardecist_spiritism "Kardecist spiritism"), which was very much in vogue at the end of the nineteenth and beginning of the twentieth century. Her experiments in spiritual investigation started in 1879.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-:0-6) She became interested in the [Theosophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theosophy "Theosophy") of [Helena Blavatsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helena_Blavatsky "Helena Blavatsky") and the philosophy of [Christian Rosenkreuz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_Rosenkreuz "Christian Rosenkreuz"). In 1908, she met [Rudolf Steiner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Steiner "Rudolf Steiner"), the founder of the [Anthroposophical Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthroposophical_Society "Anthroposophical Society"), who was visiting Stockholm.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-10) Steiner introduced her to his theories regarding the arts, and appears to have influenced her paintings later in life. Several years later, in 1920, she met Steiner again at the [Goetheanum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goetheanum "Goetheanum") in [Dornach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dornach "Dornach"), Switzerland, the headquarters of the Anthroposophical Society. Between 1921 and 1930, she spent long periods at the Goetheanum.

Af Klint's work can be understood in the wider context of the [modernist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modernist "Modernist") search for new forms in artistic, spiritual, political, and scientific systems at the beginning of the twentieth century.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-11) Other artists during this same period, including [Wassily Kandinsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wassily_Kandinsky "Wassily Kandinsky"), [Piet Mondrian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piet_Mondrian "Piet Mondrian"), [Kazimir Malevich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazimir_Malevich "Kazimir Malevich"), [Fidus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fidus "Fidus"), and the French [Les Nabis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les_Nabis "Les Nabis"), were inspired by the [Theosophical Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theosophical_Society "Theosophical Society").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-13)

The works of af Klint are mainly spiritual, and her artistic work is a consequence of this.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-14) She felt the abstract work and the meaning within were so groundbreaking that the world was not ready to see it, so she directed that the work remain unseen until twenty years after her death.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-15)

## Work

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hilma_af_Klint&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Work")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3e/Hilma_af_Klint%2C_1906-07%2C_Primordial_Chaos_-_No_16.jpg/250px-Hilma_af_Klint%2C_1906-07%2C_Primordial_Chaos_-_No_16.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hilma_af_Klint,_1906-07,_Primordial_Chaos_-_No_16.jpg)

_Primordial Chaos, No. 16_, 1906–07

At the Academy of Fine Arts she met [Anna Cassel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_Cassel "Anna Cassel"), the first of the four women with whom she later worked in "The Five" (_De Fem_), a group of artists who shared her ideas. The other members were [Cornelia Cederberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelia_Cederberg "Cornelia Cederberg"), [Sigrid Hedman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigrid_Hedman "Sigrid Hedman"), and [Mathilda Nilsson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathilda_Nilsson "Mathilda Nilsson"). The Five began their association as members of the Edelweiss Society, which embraced a combination of the Theosophical teachings of [Helena Blavatsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helena_Blavatsky "Helena Blavatsky") and spiritualism. All of _The Five_ were interested in the paranormal and regularly organized spiritistic séances.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-:0-6) They opened each meeting with a prayer, followed by a meditation, a Christian sermon, and a review and analysis of a text from the New Testament, followed by a séance.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-:0-6) They recorded in a book a completely new system of mystical thought, in the form of messages from higher spirits called _The High Masters_ ("Höga Mästare"). One Master, Gregor, announced, "All the knowledge that is not of the senses, not of the intellect, not of the heart but is the property that exclusively belongs to the deepest aspect of your being... the knowledge of your spirit".[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-16)

Through her work with The Five, Hilma af Klint created experimental [automatic drawing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surrealist_automatism#Automatic_drawing_and_painting "Surrealist automatism") as early as 1896, leading her toward an inventive geometric [visual language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_language "Visual language") capable of conceptualizing invisible forces of the inner and outer worlds.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-17) She explored world religions, atoms, and the plant world, and wrote extensively about her discoveries.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-:0-6) Af Klint created metaphors to express the messages she was receiving from the High Masters, the spirits who the artist believed used her as a conduit.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-:1-5) As she became more familiar with this form of expression, af Klint was "assigned" by the High Masters to create the paintings for the "Temple", although she said that never understood what the "Temple" referred to.

Af Klint said that she felt she was being directed by a force that would literally guide her hand. She wrote in her notebook:

> The pictures were painted directly through me, without any preliminary drawings, and with great force. I had no idea what the paintings were supposed to depict; nevertheless I worked swiftly and surely, without changing a single brush stroke.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-18)

In 1906, at the age of 44, af Klint painted her first series of abstract paintings.

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/00/Hilma_af_Klint%2C_1915%2C_Svanen%2C_No._17.jpg/250px-Hilma_af_Klint%2C_1915%2C_Svanen%2C_No._17.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hilma_af_Klint,_1915,_Svanen,_No._17.jpg)

_Svanen_ (_The Swan_), No. 17, Group 9, Series SUW, October 1914 – March 1915, a work never exhibited during af Klint's lifetime

The works for the Temple were created between 1906 and 1915, carried out in two phases, with an interruption between 1908 and 1912. Art critic [Daniel Birnbaum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Birnbaum "Daniel Birnbaum") argues that [Anna Cassel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_Cassel "Anna Cassel") likely contributed to af Klint's Temple paintings.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-19) As af Klint discovered her new form of visual expression, she developed a new artistic language. Her painting became more autonomous and more intentional. The spiritual would continue to be the main source of creativity throughout the rest of her life.

The collection for the Temple comprises 196 paintings grouped within several sub-series.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-:1-5) The major paintings, dated 1907, are large: each painting measures approximately 240 × 320 cm. This series, called _The Ten Largest_, describes the stages of life, from early childhood to old age.

Quite apart from their diagrammatic purpose, the paintings have a freshness and a modern aesthetic of tentative line and hastily captured image, such as a segmented circle, a helix bisected and divided into a spectrum of lightly painted colors. The artistic world of af Klint is infused with symbols, letters, and words. The paintings often depict symmetrical dualities or reciprocities: up and down, in and out, earthly and esoteric, male and female, good and evil. The color choice throughout is metaphorical: blue stands for the female spirit, yellow for the male one, and pink/red for physical/spiritual love. _The Swan_ and _the Dove_, names of two series of the _Paintings for the Temple_, are also symbolic, representing, respectively, transcendence and love. Understood as gates to other dimensions, her paintings call for interpretation on a narrative, esoteric, and artistic level while evoking primordial geometry and humanistic motifs.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-20)

When af Klint had completed works for the Temple, the "spiritual guidance" ended, but she continued to pursue abstract painting independent of any "external influence".[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-21) The paintings for the Temple were mostly oil paintings, but she now also used watercolors. Her later paintings are significantly smaller in size. She painted among others a series depicting the standpoints of religions at various stages in history, as well as representations of the duality between physical being and its equivalence on an esoteric level. As af Klint pursued her artistic and esoteric research, it is possible to perceive the influence of the artistic theories developed by the Anthroposophical Society. Through her life, af Klint would seek to understand the mysteries that she had felt through her work. She produced more than 150 notebooks containing her thoughts and studies.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-WITT-22)

In 1908, af Klint met [Rudolf Steiner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Steiner "Rudolf Steiner"). In one of their few remaining letters, she asked Steiner to visit her in Stockholm to see the _Paintings for the Temple_ series, 111 paintings in total. She wrote in her personal notebook:

> The execution of the work began a few years before Dr. Steiner first came to Sweden, and when I heard about him, it was immediately clear to me that he was the one who would confirm what I had perceived. Under the guidance of one, or perhaps several intelligences, the work is executed in a number of painted pictures, some very small, some very large. This logically constructed work contains an explanation of the evolution of mankind over vast periods of time. There are two reasons why I wish to interest the Anthroposophical Society in this work, namely, my absolute belief in the authenticity of the inspiration, and Dr. Steiner’s confirmation of it when, 14 or 15 years ago, he looked at the first two series then completed, on which he made a detailed explanation. Since then the work has continued, and this year I have once again personally appealed to Dr. Steiner to find out about the work. Whether it should be preserved, or whether it should be destroyed. The answer was, that it would be detrimental to let it disappear and that it could be used and useful. [[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-23)

According to [Helena Blavatsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helena_Blavatsky "Helena Blavatsky"), [mediumship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediumship "Mediumship") was a false practice, leading its adepts on the wrong paths of occultism and black magic.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-24) Steiner stated that af Klint's contemporaries would not be able to accept and understand her paintings, and that it would take another fifty years to decipher them. Of all the paintings shown to him, Steiner paid special attention only to the _Primordial Chaos_ Group, noting them as "the best symbolically".[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-:0-6) Af Klint was devastated by Steiner's response and, apparently, stopped painting for four years. Steiner kept photographs of some of af Klint's artworks, some of which were hand-coloured. Later the same year, Steiner met Wassily Kandinsky, who had not yet come to abstract painting. Some art historians assume that Kandinsky might have seen the photographs and perhaps was influenced by them while developing his own abstract path.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-IMDb-25) Later in life, af Klint made a decision to destroy all her correspondence. She left a collection of more than 1200 paintings and 125 diaries to her nephew, [Erik af Klint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erik_af_Klint_(1901%E2%80%931981) "Erik af Klint (1901–1981)"). Among her last paintings, made in the 1930s, there are two watercolors presaging the events of [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), titled _The Blitz_ and _The Fight in the Mediterranean_.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-26)

Despite the popular belief that af Klint had determined to never exhibit her abstract works during her lifetime, in recent years, art historians such as [Julia Voss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julia_Voss "Julia Voss") have uncovered evidence that af Klint did attempt to show her work. Around 1920, in Dornach, Switzerland, af Klint met Dutch [eurythmist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurythmist "Eurythmist") Peggy Kloppers-Moltzer, who was also a member of The [Anthroposophical Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthroposophical_Society "Anthroposophical Society"). Later, the artist travelled to Amsterdam, where she and Kloppers discussed a possible exhibition with the editors of the art and architecture magazine _[Wendingen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wendingen "Wendingen")_. Although the Amsterdam talks were not successful, at least one exhibition of af Klint's abstract works took place in London several years later, in 1928, at the World Conference on Spiritual Science in London, for which Kloppers was a member of the organizing committee. Originally, af Klint was excluded, but after Kloppers' insistence, she was added to the list of participants.

In July 1928, af Klint sailed from Stockholm to London, taking along some of her large-scale paintings. In her postcard to [Anna Cassel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_Cassel "Anna Cassel") (discovered in 2018), af Klint wrote that she was not alone during this four-day trip. Despite af Klint not having named her traveling companion, Julia Voss suggests that it was most likely Thomasine Andersson, an old friend from her De Fem days. Voss also suggests that it is probable that the works were from the _Paintings for the Temple_ series.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-27)

In 1944, Hilma af Klint died at age 81 in [Djursholm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Djursholm "Djursholm"), Sweden,[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-Phaidon_Editors-28) after a traffic accident. She had exhibited her work only a handful of times, for the most part at spiritual conferences and gatherings.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-29) She is buried at [Galärvarvskyrkogården](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gal%C3%A4rvarvskyrkog%C3%A5rden "Galärvarvskyrkogården") in Stockholm.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-30)

## Signature style

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hilma_af_Klint&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Signature style")]

Af Klint's later period abstract art (1906–1920) delved into symbolism employing a combination of geometry, figuration, scientific research, and religious practices. Her studies of organic growth, including shells and flowers, infused her portrayals life through a spiritual lens.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-31)

Af Klint's individual or signature [style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Style_(visual_arts) "Style (visual arts)") was also marked with impressions from late 19th and early 20th century scientific discoveries as influenced by contemporary spiritual movements such as [theosophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theosophy "Theosophy") and [anthroposophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthroposophy "Anthroposophy"). The notion of transcending the physical world and the constraints of representational art is visible in her abstract paintings.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-32) Britt Lundgren theorized that af Klint was influenced by the work of the scientist [Thomas Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Young_(scientist) "Thomas Young (scientist)"), whose writings were known to the Theosophists.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-33)

Af Klint's symbolic visual language has an ordered progression that reflects her understanding of grids, circles, spirals and petal-like forms—sometimes diagrammatic, sometimes biomorphic.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-34) Her paintings also explore the dichotomies she saw in the world.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-35) Spiral forms appear often in her art, as they do in the [automatic drawings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surrealist_automatism#Automatic_drawing_and_painting "Surrealist automatism") by [De Fem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Fem "De Fem"). While every geometric form suggests growth, progress, and evolution, her color choices were also intended to be metaphorical in nature.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-36) As one of the Proto-Feminist Artists, her style represents the [sublime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sublime_(philosophy) "Sublime (philosophy)") in art.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-37)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hilma_af_Klint&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Hilma af Klint never married, lived only with women, and prioritized deep friendships with them. She left no diary entries or letters that suggest romantic relationships. Modern speculation is that she was queer or lesbian, and that her paintings and views on [androgyny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Androgyny "Androgyny") and [gender fluidity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gender_fluidity "Gender fluidity") show queer sensibility. Af Klint's decision to keep her work secret for twenty years after her death has prompted comparisons with [Emily Dickinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emily_Dickinson "Emily Dickinson").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-39)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-40)

## Legacy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hilma_af_Klint&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Legacy")]

In her will, Hilma af Klint left all her abstract paintings to her nephew, Vice Admiral [Erik af Klint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erik_af_Klint_(1901%E2%80%931981) "Erik af Klint (1901–1981)") of the [Royal Swedish Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_Navy "Swedish Navy"). She specified that her work should be kept secret for at least twenty years after her death. When the boxes were opened at the end of the 1960s, very few persons had knowledge of what would be revealed.

In 1970, her paintings were offered as a gift to [Moderna Museet i Stockholm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moderna_Museet "Moderna Museet"), but the donation was declined. Erik af Klint then donated thousands of drawings and paintings to a foundation bearing the artist's name.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-auto-41) Thanks to the art historian Åke Fant, her art was introduced to an international audience in the 1980s, when he presented her at a [Nordik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nordik "Nordik") conference in [Helsinki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helsinki "Helsinki") in 1984.

The collection of abstract paintings of Hilma af Klint includes more than 1200 pieces, owned and managed by the Hilma af Klint Foundation[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-42) in Stockholm, Sweden. In 2017, Norwegian architectural firm [Snøhetta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sn%C3%B8hetta_(company) "Snøhetta (company)") presented plans for an exhibition space dedicated to af Klint in [Järna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C3%A4rna,_S%C3%B6dert%C3%A4lje_Municipality "Järna, Södertälje Municipality"), south of Stockholm, with estimated building costs of €6 to 7.5 million.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-auto-41) In February 2018, the Foundation signed a longterm agreement of cooperation with the Moderna Museet, where her works had been refused less than forty years earlier, thereby confirming the permanence of the Hilma af Klint Room as a space at the museum where a dozen works of the artist are shown on a continuous basis.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-43)

Af Klint's work was included in the 2021 exhibition _[Women in Abstraction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women\_in\_Abstraction "Women in Abstraction")_ at the [Centre Pompidou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centre_Pompidou "Centre Pompidou").[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-Women_in_abstraction-44)

"af Klint" redirects here. For other uses, see [af Klint (disambiguation)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Af_Klint_(disambiguation) "Af Klint (disambiguation)").

**Hilma af Klint** (Swedish:[[ˈhɪ̂lːma ˈɑːv ˈklɪnːt]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Swedish "Help:IPA/Swedish"); 26 October 1862 – 21 October 1944) was a Swedish [artist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artist "Artist") and [mystic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mysticism "Mysticism") whose paintings are considered to be among the first major [abstract](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstract_art "Abstract art") works in Western art history.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-1) A considerable body of her work predates the first purely abstract compositions by [Kandinsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wassily_Kandinsky "Wassily Kandinsky"), [Malevich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazimir_Malevich "Kazimir Malevich"), and [Mondrian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piet_Mondrian "Piet Mondrian").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-TATE-2) She belonged to a group called "The Five", a circle of women inspired by [Theosophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theosophy "Theosophy") who shared a belief in the importance of trying to contact the "[High Masters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masters_of_the_Ancient_Wisdom "Masters of the Ancient Wisdom")", often through [séances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A9ance "Séance").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-3) Her paintings, which sometimes resemble diagrams, were a visual representation of complex spiritual ideas.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-4)

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hilma_af_Klint&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/94/Eftersommar_Hilma_af_Klint_1903.jpeg/500px-Eftersommar_Hilma_af_Klint_1903.jpeg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Eftersommar_Hilma_af_Klint_1903.jpeg)

_Eftersommar_ (_Late Summer_) an early naturalistic work, painted by af Klint in 1903, an example of the works she exhibited to the public during her lifetime

Hilma af Klint was the fourth child of Mathilda ([née](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_name#Maiden_and_married_names "Birth name")Sonntag) and Captain Victor af Klint, a Swedish naval commander. The family surname is 'af Klint', _af_ being a Swedish [nobiliary particle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobiliary_particle "Nobiliary particle"). She spent summers with her family at their manor, "Hanmora", on the island of [Adelsö](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adels%C3%B6 "Adelsö") on [Lake Mälaren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_M%C3%A4laren "Lake Mälaren"). In these idyllic surroundings, she came into contact with nature at an early age. Her experience of natural forms became an inspiration in her work, and she later lived on [Munsö](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muns%C3%B6 "Munsö"), an island next to Adelsö.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Af Klint showed a great interest in [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics "Mathematics") and [botany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Botany "Botany") and an ability in visual art. After the family moved to Stockholm, she studied at _Tekniska skolan_ (Technical School, now [Konstfack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Konstfack "Konstfack")) in Stockholm, where she studied portraiture and landscape painting.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-:1-5)

Af Klint was admitted to the [Royal Academy of Fine Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Swedish_Academy_of_Fine_Arts "Royal Swedish Academy of Fine Arts") at the age of twenty.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-:0-6) Between 1882 and 1887, she studied portrait painting, botanical drawing, and landscape painting.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-:1-5) She graduated with honors and was granted a scholarship in the form of a studio in the "Atelier Building" (Ateljébyggnaden) owned by the Academy of Fine Arts between [Hamngatan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamngatan "Hamngatan") and [Kungsträdgården](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kungstr%C3%A4dg%C3%A5rden "Kungsträdgården") in central Stockholm, which was the main cultural hub in the Swedish capital at that time. The same building also held [Blanch's Café](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blanch's_Caf%C3%A9 "Blanch's Café") and Blanch's Art Gallery, where conflict arose between the conventional views of the Academy of Fine Arts and the opposition movement of the Art Society ([Konstnärsförbundet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Konstn%C3%A4rsf%C3%B6rbundet "Konstnärsförbundet")), inspired by the French [_plein air_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/En_plein_air "En plein air") painters. Af Klint began working in Stockholm, gaining recognition for her landscapes, botanical drawings, and portraits.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-7) Her conventional painting was a source of income, but her abstract remained a separate practice.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-8)

## Spiritual and philosophical ideas

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hilma_af_Klint&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Spiritual and philosophical ideas")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6d/Hilma-af-Klint.jpg/250px-Hilma-af-Klint.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hilma-af-Klint.jpg)

af Klint in her studio, c. 1895

In 1880, af Klint's younger sister Hermina died. Around this time, the spiritual dimension of her life had begun to develop.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-9) Af Klint's interest in abstraction and symbolism grew from her involvement in [spiritism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kardecist_spiritism "Kardecist spiritism"), which was very much in vogue at the end of the nineteenth and beginning of the twentieth century. Her experiments in spiritual investigation started in 1879.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-:0-6) She became interested in the [Theosophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theosophy "Theosophy") of [Helena Blavatsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helena_Blavatsky "Helena Blavatsky") and the philosophy of [Christian Rosenkreuz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_Rosenkreuz "Christian Rosenkreuz"). In 1908, she met [Rudolf Steiner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Steiner "Rudolf Steiner"), the founder of the [Anthroposophical Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthroposophical_Society "Anthroposophical Society"), who was visiting Stockholm.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-10) Steiner introduced her to his theories regarding the arts, and appears to have influenced her paintings later in life. Several years later, in 1920, she met Steiner again at the [Goetheanum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goetheanum "Goetheanum") in [Dornach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dornach "Dornach"), Switzerland, the headquarters of the Anthroposophical Society. Between 1921 and 1930, she spent long periods at the Goetheanum.

Af Klint's work can be understood in the wider context of the [modernist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modernist "Modernist") search for new forms in artistic, spiritual, political, and scientific systems at the beginning of the twentieth century.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-11) Other artists during this same period, including [Wassily Kandinsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wassily_Kandinsky "Wassily Kandinsky"), [Piet Mondrian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piet_Mondrian "Piet Mondrian"), [Kazimir Malevich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazimir_Malevich "Kazimir Malevich"), [Fidus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fidus "Fidus"), and the French [Les Nabis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les_Nabis "Les Nabis"), were inspired by the [Theosophical Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theosophical_Society "Theosophical Society").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-13)

The works of af Klint are mainly spiritual, and her artistic work is a consequence of this.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-14) She felt the abstract work and the meaning within were so groundbreaking that the world was not ready to see it, so she directed that the work remain unseen until twenty years after her death.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-15)

## Work

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hilma_af_Klint&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Work")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3e/Hilma_af_Klint%2C_1906-07%2C_Primordial_Chaos_-_No_16.jpg/250px-Hilma_af_Klint%2C_1906-07%2C_Primordial_Chaos_-_No_16.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hilma_af_Klint,_1906-07,_Primordial_Chaos_-_No_16.jpg)

_Primordial Chaos, No. 16_, 1906–07

At the Academy of Fine Arts she met [Anna Cassel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_Cassel "Anna Cassel"), the first of the four women with whom she later worked in "The Five" (_De Fem_), a group of artists who shared her ideas. The other members were [Cornelia Cederberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelia_Cederberg "Cornelia Cederberg"), [Sigrid Hedman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigrid_Hedman "Sigrid Hedman"), and [Mathilda Nilsson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathilda_Nilsson "Mathilda Nilsson"). The Five began their association as members of the Edelweiss Society, which embraced a combination of the Theosophical teachings of [Helena Blavatsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helena_Blavatsky "Helena Blavatsky") and spiritualism. All of _The Five_ were interested in the paranormal and regularly organized spiritistic séances.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-:0-6) They opened each meeting with a prayer, followed by a meditation, a Christian sermon, and a review and analysis of a text from the New Testament, followed by a séance.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-:0-6) They recorded in a book a completely new system of mystical thought, in the form of messages from higher spirits called _The High Masters_ ("Höga Mästare"). One Master, Gregor, announced, "All the knowledge that is not of the senses, not of the intellect, not of the heart but is the property that exclusively belongs to the deepest aspect of your being... the knowledge of your spirit".[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-16)

Through her work with The Five, Hilma af Klint created experimental [automatic drawing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surrealist_automatism#Automatic_drawing_and_painting "Surrealist automatism") as early as 1896, leading her toward an inventive geometric [visual language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_language "Visual language") capable of conceptualizing invisible forces of the inner and outer worlds.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-17) She explored world religions, atoms, and the plant world, and wrote extensively about her discoveries.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-:0-6) Af Klint created metaphors to express the messages she was receiving from the High Masters, the spirits who the artist believed used her as a conduit.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-:1-5) As she became more familiar with this form of expression, af Klint was "assigned" by the High Masters to create the paintings for the "Temple", although she said that never understood what the "Temple" referred to.

Af Klint said that she felt she was being directed by a force that would literally guide her hand. She wrote in her notebook:

> The pictures were painted directly through me, without any preliminary drawings, and with great force. I had no idea what the paintings were supposed to depict; nevertheless I worked swiftly and surely, without changing a single brush stroke.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-18)

In 1906, at the age of 44, af Klint painted her first series of abstract paintings.

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/00/Hilma_af_Klint%2C_1915%2C_Svanen%2C_No._17.jpg/250px-Hilma_af_Klint%2C_1915%2C_Svanen%2C_No._17.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hilma_af_Klint,_1915,_Svanen,_No._17.jpg)

_Svanen_ (_The Swan_), No. 17, Group 9, Series SUW, October 1914 – March 1915, a work never exhibited during af Klint's lifetime

The works for the Temple were created between 1906 and 1915, carried out in two phases, with an interruption between 1908 and 1912. Art critic [Daniel Birnbaum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Birnbaum "Daniel Birnbaum") argues that [Anna Cassel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_Cassel "Anna Cassel") likely contributed to af Klint's Temple paintings.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-19) As af Klint discovered her new form of visual expression, she developed a new artistic language. Her painting became more autonomous and more intentional. The spiritual would continue to be the main source of creativity throughout the rest of her life.

The collection for the Temple comprises 196 paintings grouped within several sub-series.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-:1-5) The major paintings, dated 1907, are large: each painting measures approximately 240 × 320 cm. This series, called _The Ten Largest_, describes the stages of life, from early childhood to old age.

Quite apart from their diagrammatic purpose, the paintings have a freshness and a modern aesthetic of tentative line and hastily captured image, such as a segmented circle, a helix bisected and divided into a spectrum of lightly painted colors. The artistic world of af Klint is infused with symbols, letters, and words. The paintings often depict symmetrical dualities or reciprocities: up and down, in and out, earthly and esoteric, male and female, good and evil. The color choice throughout is metaphorical: blue stands for the female spirit, yellow for the male one, and pink/red for physical/spiritual love. _The Swan_ and _the Dove_, names of two series of the _Paintings for the Temple_, are also symbolic, representing, respectively, transcendence and love. Understood as gates to other dimensions, her paintings call for interpretation on a narrative, esoteric, and artistic level while evoking primordial geometry and humanistic motifs.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-20)

When af Klint had completed works for the Temple, the "spiritual guidance" ended, but she continued to pursue abstract painting independent of any "external influence".[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-21) The paintings for the Temple were mostly oil paintings, but she now also used watercolors. Her later paintings are significantly smaller in size. She painted among others a series depicting the standpoints of religions at various stages in history, as well as representations of the duality between physical being and its equivalence on an esoteric level. As af Klint pursued her artistic and esoteric research, it is possible to perceive the influence of the artistic theories developed by the Anthroposophical Society. Through her life, af Klint would seek to understand the mysteries that she had felt through her work. She produced more than 150 notebooks containing her thoughts and studies.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-WITT-22)

In 1908, af Klint met [Rudolf Steiner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Steiner "Rudolf Steiner"). In one of their few remaining letters, she asked Steiner to visit her in Stockholm to see the _Paintings for the Temple_ series, 111 paintings in total. She wrote in her personal notebook:

> The execution of the work began a few years before Dr. Steiner first came to Sweden, and when I heard about him, it was immediately clear to me that he was the one who would confirm what I had perceived. Under the guidance of one, or perhaps several intelligences, the work is executed in a number of painted pictures, some very small, some very large. This logically constructed work contains an explanation of the evolution of mankind over vast periods of time. There are two reasons why I wish to interest the Anthroposophical Society in this work, namely, my absolute belief in the authenticity of the inspiration, and Dr. Steiner’s confirmation of it when, 14 or 15 years ago, he looked at the first two series then completed, on which he made a detailed explanation. Since then the work has continued, and this year I have once again personally appealed to Dr. Steiner to find out about the work. Whether it should be preserved, or whether it should be destroyed. The answer was, that it would be detrimental to let it disappear and that it could be used and useful. [[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-23)

According to [Helena Blavatsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helena_Blavatsky "Helena Blavatsky"), [mediumship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediumship "Mediumship") was a false practice, leading its adepts on the wrong paths of occultism and black magic.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-24) Steiner stated that af Klint's contemporaries would not be able to accept and understand her paintings, and that it would take another fifty years to decipher them. Of all the paintings shown to him, Steiner paid special attention only to the _Primordial Chaos_ Group, noting them as "the best symbolically".[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-:0-6) Af Klint was devastated by Steiner's response and, apparently, stopped painting for four years. Steiner kept photographs of some of af Klint's artworks, some of which were hand-coloured. Later the same year, Steiner met Wassily Kandinsky, who had not yet come to abstract painting. Some art historians assume that Kandinsky might have seen the photographs and perhaps was influenced by them while developing his own abstract path.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-IMDb-25) Later in life, af Klint made a decision to destroy all her correspondence. She left a collection of more than 1200 paintings and 125 diaries to her nephew, [Erik af Klint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erik_af_Klint_(1901%E2%80%931981) "Erik af Klint (1901–1981)"). Among her last paintings, made in the 1930s, there are two watercolors presaging the events of [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), titled _The Blitz_ and _The Fight in the Mediterranean_.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-26)

Despite the popular belief that af Klint had determined to never exhibit her abstract works during her lifetime, in recent years, art historians such as [Julia Voss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julia_Voss "Julia Voss") have uncovered evidence that af Klint did attempt to show her work. Around 1920, in Dornach, Switzerland, af Klint met Dutch [eurythmist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurythmist "Eurythmist") Peggy Kloppers-Moltzer, who was also a member of The [Anthroposophical Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthroposophical_Society "Anthroposophical Society"). Later, the artist travelled to Amsterdam, where she and Kloppers discussed a possible exhibition with the editors of the art and architecture magazine _[Wendingen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wendingen "Wendingen")_. Although the Amsterdam talks were not successful, at least one exhibition of af Klint's abstract works took place in London several years later, in 1928, at the World Conference on Spiritual Science in London, for which Kloppers was a member of the organizing committee. Originally, af Klint was excluded, but after Kloppers' insistence, she was added to the list of participants.

In July 1928, af Klint sailed from Stockholm to London, taking along some of her large-scale paintings. In her postcard to [Anna Cassel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_Cassel "Anna Cassel") (discovered in 2018), af Klint wrote that she was not alone during this four-day trip. Despite af Klint not having named her traveling companion, Julia Voss suggests that it was most likely Thomasine Andersson, an old friend from her De Fem days. Voss also suggests that it is probable that the works were from the _Paintings for the Temple_ series.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-27)

In 1944, Hilma af Klint died at age 81 in [Djursholm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Djursholm "Djursholm"), Sweden,[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-Phaidon_Editors-28) after a traffic accident. She had exhibited her work only a handful of times, for the most part at spiritual conferences and gatherings.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-29) She is buried at [Galärvarvskyrkogården](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gal%C3%A4rvarvskyrkog%C3%A5rden "Galärvarvskyrkogården") in Stockholm.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-30)

## Signature style

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hilma_af_Klint&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Signature style")]

Af Klint's later period abstract art (1906–1920) delved into symbolism employing a combination of geometry, figuration, scientific research, and religious practices. Her studies of organic growth, including shells and flowers, infused her portrayals life through a spiritual lens.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-31)

Af Klint's individual or signature [style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Style_(visual_arts) "Style (visual arts)") was also marked with impressions from late 19th and early 20th century scientific discoveries as influenced by contemporary spiritual movements such as [theosophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theosophy "Theosophy") and [anthroposophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthroposophy "Anthroposophy"). The notion of transcending the physical world and the constraints of representational art is visible in her abstract paintings.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-32) Britt Lundgren theorized that af Klint was influenced by the work of the scientist [Thomas Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Young_(scientist) "Thomas Young (scientist)"), whose writings were known to the Theosophists.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-33)

Af Klint's symbolic visual language has an ordered progression that reflects her understanding of grids, circles, spirals and petal-like forms—sometimes diagrammatic, sometimes biomorphic.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-34) Her paintings also explore the dichotomies she saw in the world.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-35) Spiral forms appear often in her art, as they do in the [automatic drawings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surrealist_automatism#Automatic_drawing_and_painting "Surrealist automatism") by [De Fem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Fem "De Fem"). While every geometric form suggests growth, progress, and evolution, her color choices were also intended to be metaphorical in nature.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-36) As one of the Proto-Feminist Artists, her style represents the [sublime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sublime_(philosophy) "Sublime (philosophy)") in art.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-37)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hilma_af_Klint&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Hilma af Klint never married, lived only with women, and prioritized deep friendships with them. She left no diary entries or letters that suggest romantic relationships. Modern speculation is that she was queer or lesbian, and that her paintings and views on [androgyny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Androgyny "Androgyny") and [gender fluidity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gender_fluidity "Gender fluidity") show queer sensibility. Af Klint's decision to keep her work secret for twenty years after her death has prompted comparisons with [Emily Dickinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emily_Dickinson "Emily Dickinson").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-39)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-40)

## Legacy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hilma_af_Klint&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Legacy")]

In her will, Hilma af Klint left all her abstract paintings to her nephew, Vice Admiral [Erik af Klint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erik_af_Klint_(1901%E2%80%931981) "Erik af Klint (1901–1981)") of the [Royal Swedish Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_Navy "Swedish Navy"). She specified that her work should be kept secret for at least twenty years after her death. When the boxes were opened at the end of the 1960s, very few persons had knowledge of what would be revealed.

In 1970, her paintings were offered as a gift to [Moderna Museet i Stockholm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moderna_Museet "Moderna Museet"), but the donation was declined. Erik af Klint then donated thousands of drawings and paintings to a foundation bearing the artist's name.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-auto-41) Thanks to the art historian Åke Fant, her art was introduced to an international audience in the 1980s, when he presented her at a [Nordik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nordik "Nordik") conference in [Helsinki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helsinki "Helsinki") in 1984.

The collection of abstract paintings of Hilma af Klint includes more than 1200 pieces, owned and managed by the Hilma af Klint Foundation[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-42) in Stockholm, Sweden. In 2017, Norwegian architectural firm [Snøhetta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sn%C3%B8hetta_(company) "Snøhetta (company)") presented plans for an exhibition space dedicated to af Klint in [Järna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C3%A4rna,_S%C3%B6dert%C3%A4lje_Municipality "Järna, Södertälje Municipality"), south of Stockholm, with estimated building costs of €6 to 7.5 million.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-auto-41) In February 2018, the Foundation signed a longterm agreement of cooperation with the Moderna Museet, where her works had been refused less than forty years earlier, thereby confirming the permanence of the Hilma af Klint Room as a space at the museum where a dozen works of the artist are shown on a continuous basis.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-43)

Af Klint's work was included in the 2021 exhibition _[Women in Abstraction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women\_in\_Abstraction "Women in Abstraction")_ at the [Centre Pompidou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centre_Pompidou "Centre Pompidou").[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilma_af_Klint#cite_note-Women_in_abstraction-44)

# Hilma af Klint

The Ten Largest

22.9 2022–8.1 2023

Stockholm

 Meet Hilma af Klint and her series of paintings “The Ten Largest”, when the works are once again on show in the museum in autumn 2022. This time the paintings will be exhibited together with a selection of the artist’s watercolours and a complete collection of hand-coloured photographs of “The Ten Largest” that has never previously been shown in its entirety.

## About the exhibition

It was autumn 1907 when the Swedish artist Hilma af Klint (1862–1944) began the first canvas in a series that would come to be known as “The Ten Largest”. Working on these ten paintings over a period of just 40 days, the result she produced is one of the most monumental legacies of her artistic output. The series is part of a larger collection known as “Paintings for the Temple”, a mammoth project that the artist had embarked upon two years earlier after experiencing non-verbal cues from the spirit world. The challenge of understanding these messages and finding a visual expression for an invisible reality was to preoccupy Hilma af Klint throughout the rest of her life.

Throughout her life, Hilma af Klint sought the right context for her paintings and only showed them to a limited number of people while waiting for the world to become ready to receive their message. Today, more than a hundred years later, her work is acclaimed all over the world.

![Image 15:  Squares in red, blue and yellow against a light pink background](https://www.modernamuseet.se/app/uploads/stockholm/2022/09/af-klint-hilma_grupp-iv-nr-10-de-tio-strsta-lderdomen-1907_f_albin-dahlstrom.jpg)

Hilma af Klint, De tio största, nr 10, Ålderdomen, grupp IV, 1907 © Stiftelsen Hilma af Klints Verk. Photo: Albin Dahlström / Moderna Museet

### Evolution and spirit worlds

The sheer size of “The Ten Largest” sets them apart from the artist’s other works. In a gigantic 3.28×2.40 metre format, Hilma af Klint celebrates the four ages of humanity: Childhood, Youth, Adulthood and Old Age.

A central theme in “The Ten Largest”, as in the artist’s oeuvre as a whole, is the notion of evolution. Hilma af Klint, however, seems less concerned about evolution in terms of any physical development from one form of existence to another, and focuses instead on evolution on a spiritual plane.

This reflects an interest in spirituality and theosophy that she shared with many of her contemporaries.

### Close collaboration with The Hilma af Klint Foundation

Thanks to the close collaboration between Moderna Museet and [The Hilma af Klint Foundation](https://hilmaafklint.se/), in autumn 2022 visitors to the Museum can renew their acquaintance with “The Ten Largest” by Hilma af Klint, showing in Stockholm for the first time since 2013.

The exhibition also includes a selection of watercolours and a collection of hand-coloured photographs that has never previously been on public display in its entirety.

## About the exhibition

It was autumn 1907 when the Swedish artist Hilma af Klint (1862–1944) began the first canvas in a series that would come to be known as “The Ten Largest”. Working on these ten paintings over a period of just 40 days, the result she produced is one of the most monumental legacies of her artistic output. The series is part of a larger collection known as “Paintings for the Temple”, a mammoth project that the artist had embarked upon two years earlier after experiencing non-verbal cues from the spirit world. The challenge of understanding these messages and finding a visual expression for an invisible reality was to preoccupy Hilma af Klint throughout the rest of her life.

Throughout her life, Hilma af Klint sought the right context for her paintings and only showed them to a limited number of people while waiting for the world to become ready to receive their message. Today, more than a hundred years later, her work is acclaimed all over the world.

![Image 15:  Squares in red, blue and yellow against a light pink background](https://www.modernamuseet.se/app/uploads/stockholm/2022/09/af-klint-hilma_grupp-iv-nr-10-de-tio-strsta-lderdomen-1907_f_albin-dahlstrom.jpg)

Hilma af Klint, De tio största, nr 10, Ålderdomen, grupp IV, 1907 © Stiftelsen Hilma af Klints Verk. Photo: Albin Dahlström / Moderna Museet

### Evolution and spirit worlds

The sheer size of “The Ten Largest” sets them apart from the artist’s other works. In a gigantic 3.28×2.40 metre format, Hilma af Klint celebrates the four ages of humanity: Childhood, Youth, Adulthood and Old Age.

A central theme in “The Ten Largest”, as in the artist’s oeuvre as a whole, is the notion of evolution. Hilma af Klint, however, seems less concerned about evolution in terms of any physical development from one form of existence to another, and focuses instead on evolution on a spiritual plane.

This reflects an interest in spirituality and theosophy that she shared with many of her contemporaries.

### Close collaboration with The Hilma af Klint Foundation

Thanks to the close collaboration between Moderna Museet and [The Hilma af Klint Foundation](https://hilmaafklint.se/), in autumn 2022 visitors to the Museum can renew their acquaintance with “The Ten Largest” by Hilma af Klint, showing in Stockholm for the first time since 2013.

The exhibition also includes a selection of watercolours and a collection of hand-coloured photographs that has never previously been on public display in its entirety.
